title: Leasehold conveyancing I: the grant and structure of a lease
subtitle: The term of years absolute, fixtures on exit, and grant versus assignment
objectives: Explain why a term of years absolute is capable of existing as a legal estate under s 1(1)(b) LPA 1925
Apply the fixtures rule to distinguish what a tenant may remove at the end of a term from what must stay
Distinguish the grant of a new lease from the assignment of an existing one, and explain why the conveyancing steps differ

leadingAuthorities.role: Lists a term of years absolute among the estates capable of existing as a legal estate in land
Sets out the tests for distinguishing a fixture from a chattel

whyThisMattersTemplate.default: This is the lesson that sets up everything else in the leasehold sequence — get the grant/assignment distinction and the legal-estate point wrong here and every later lesson on rent review, alienation and forfeiture will be built on the wrong foundation.

profileHooks.weakApplication: You know the definitions already. The test pool below focuses on telling a grant from an assignment on the facts, and applying the fixtures test to specific items — expect scenarios, not labels.
profileHooks.weakKnowledge: Take Parts 1 and 2 slowly — the term of years absolute and the grant/assignment distinction are the two ideas the rest of this lesson, and the leasehold lessons after it, are built on.

overview.hook: A tenant leaves at the end of a ten-year lease and takes the light fittings, the built-in bookshelves, and a decorative fireplace surround her grandmother gave her. Two of those are hers to take. One isn't — and the difference has nothing to do with sentiment or who paid for it. It turns on a test a court set down decades ago, and it decides who owns what the moment a lease ends.

parts.heading: The term of years absolute as a legal estate
parts.voice: structural — places leasehold within the statutory scheme before going further
body: Section 1(1) of the Law of Property Act 1925 is short and does a great deal of work: it lists only two estates capable of existing as legal estates in land. The first is the fee simple absolute in possession — freehold. The second, at s 1(1)(b), is the term of years absolute — leasehold.

Everything else — a life interest, an interest in remainder, most other rights over land — can only ever exist in equity. A lease, by contrast, sits alongside freehold as one of only two ways to hold a legal estate at all, provided it satisfies the basic requirements: certainty of term (a fixed maximum duration, even if it can be brought to an early end) and exclusive possession granted to the tenant.

This is why leasehold conveyancing is treated as its own discipline rather than a variant of freehold conveyancing. A lease is not simply a long licence to occupy — it is a distinct legal estate in the land itself, capable of being bought, sold, mortgaged and inherited in broadly the same way a freehold can, which is precisely what makes the grant and assignment of leases a conveyancing transaction in its own right.

components.text: The only estates in land which are capable of subsisting or of being conveyed or created at law are (a) an estate in fee simple absolute in possession; (b) a term of years absolute.
elements: All other interests in land exist only in equity

interaction.prompt: Under s 1(1) LPA 1925, how many estates are capable of existing as legal estates in land?
options: One
Two
Three
As many as the parties agree by contract
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right — the fee simple absolute in possession and the term of years absolute are the only two; everything else is equitable only.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Only two. Section 1(1) is deliberately exhaustive: the fee simple absolute in possession (freehold) and the term of years absolute (leasehold) — nothing else can exist as a legal estate.

parts.heading: Grant versus assignment: the two ways a lease reaches a tenant
parts.voice: compare-and-contrast — sets the two transactions side by side early
body: A tenant can come to hold a lease in one of two fundamentally different ways, and confusing them is one of the most consequential errors a trainee can make, because the conveyancing steps genuinely differ between them.

The grant of a lease is the creation of a brand-new legal estate: a landlord who owns the freehold (or a superior leasehold interest) carves a term of years out of it and grants that new term to a tenant for the first time. Nothing existed before; the lease is created by the grant itself.

The assignment of a lease is entirely different: it is the transfer of an existing lease — one already granted, with time still left to run — from a current tenant (the assignor) to a new tenant (the assignee). No new estate is created. The assignee simply steps into a lease that already exists, subject to whatever obligations already bind it.

components.label: Grant vs assignment: what actually differs
points: Grant: landlord creates a brand-new term of years and gives it to a tenant for the first time
Assignment: an existing tenant transfers a lease that is already running to a new tenant
Grant conveyancing centres on negotiating and drafting the lease terms from scratch
Assignment conveyancing centres on due diligence into the existing lease and dealing with any landlord's consent required to assign

interaction.prompt: Which scenario describes an assignment rather than a grant?
interaction.scenarioA: A landlord who owns the freehold of an office building signs a new 15-year lease with a tenant who has never occupied the building before.
interaction.scenarioB: A tenant with 8 years left on their existing 15-year lease sells their remaining interest in it to a new tenant, who takes over the lease as it stands.
interaction.explanation: B is an assignment: the lease already exists and the current tenant transfers it, with the remaining term unchanged, to a new tenant. A is a grant: the landlord is creating a brand-new term of years that never previously existed.

parts.heading: Why the conveyancing steps genuinely differ
parts.voice: practical — follows each transaction through its distinctive steps
body: On a grant, the solicitor's work is substantially about drafting and negotiation: agreeing the term, the rent, the repairing obligations, any rent review or break clause, and the extent of what is actually demised. There is no existing document to investigate — the lease is being built from nothing, usually starting from a draft the landlord's solicitor produces.

On an assignment, the lease terms are already fixed and cannot be renegotiated as part of the transaction — the assignee simply takes on the existing lease's obligations. The conveyancing work instead centres on due diligence: checking the lease for any covenant against assignment without landlord's consent (an alienation clause), obtaining that consent (often through a formal licence to assign) where required, and confirming the current tenant is not in breach of any of its own obligations before the new tenant takes over.

This distinction carries forward across the rest of the leasehold syllabus. Rent review and repairing covenants are usually a grant-stage drafting question; alienation clauses and licences to assign are usually an assignment-stage due diligence question. Misreading which transaction is in front of you leads directly to doing the wrong kind of work.

components.definition: A landlord's formal consent, required under many leases before a tenant may assign, permitting a specific assignment to a specific assignee — distinct from, and usually a precondition to, the assignment itself taking effect.

interaction.prompt: Tap the fact that shows this transaction is an assignment rather than a grant.
interaction.scenarioText: A commercial tenant with 6 years remaining on its existing 10-year lease wants to transfer the premises to another business. The lease contains an alienation clause requiring landlord's consent. The tenant's solicitor obtains a licence to assign before the transfer completes, and the new tenant takes over the lease with 6 years left to run.
tappableSpans: 6 years remaining on its existing 10-year lease
contains an alienation clause requiring landlord's consent
takes over the lease with 6 years left to run
interaction.correctSpan: 6 years remaining on its existing 10-year lease
interaction.feedbackCorrect: That's the key fact — an existing lease with time left to run is being transferred, not a brand-new term being created. Everything else (the alienation clause, the licence to assign) follows from that.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Look for the fact that shows a lease already exists before this transaction starts, rather than one being created by it. The existing 6 years remaining on a 10-year term is what marks this out as an assignment.

parts.heading: Fixtures: what stays, and what the tenant may take
parts.voice: worked-example — applies the legal test to concrete objects
body: When a lease ends, a dispute frequently arises over what the outgoing tenant may remove. The starting position is that anything which has become a fixture — annexed to the land or building so as to form part of it — belongs to the landlord and must stay; anything that remains a chattel belongs to the tenant and goes with them.

Berkley v Poulett set out the modern test for telling the two apart, using two linked questions: the degree of annexation (how firmly, and by what means, is the item attached?) and the purpose of annexation (was it fixed there to improve the land or building permanently, or merely to enjoy the item better as a chattel?). Neither question is decisive alone — a heavy item resting under its own weight can still be a fixture if its purpose was to improve the property, and a lightly screwed-in item can remain a chattel if its purpose was purely to display or use it as an object.

In that case, a large freestanding statue held in place only by its own weight was found to remain a chattel, while a stone plinth cemented into position was held to have become a fixture — even though the plinth might seem the less obviously important object. Degree of annexation without the right purpose does not automatically convert an item into a fixture, and purpose without any real annexation does not do so either; the two questions have to be read together.

components.factsShort: A dispute over items removed from a country house on sale, including paintings fixed to panelling, a statue on a plinth, and a sundial, turned on which were fixtures passing with the land and which remained chattels.
components.ratioShort: Whether an item is a fixture depends on both the degree of annexation to the land and the purpose of that annexation — an item resting by its own weight can still be a fixture if fixed there to improve the property permanently.

expanded.facts: On the sale of a country estate, a dispute arose over several items: pictures that had been fitted into recesses in wall panelling, a large statue on a stone plinth in the garden (the statue resting on the plinth by its own weight, the plinth itself cemented to a base), and a sundial. The question was which passed to the buyer as fixtures and which the seller could remove as chattels.
expanded.judgmentExtract: The court held that the degree of annexation and the purpose of annexation must both be considered, and that the purpose test had become the more important of the two in modern law. An item is more likely to be a fixture if it was fixed with the object of permanently improving the land or building, and less likely to be a fixture if it was fixed only so it could be enjoyed as an item in itself.
expanded.significance: Berkley v Poulett remains the leading modern statement of the fixtures test, regularly applied in leasehold cases to determine what an outgoing tenant may remove at the end of a term and what must be left for the landlord.

interaction.prompt: A tenant leaving rented premises wants to take a heavy bookcase that was never fixed to the wall and simply stands under its own weight against it. Applying Berkley v Poulett, is the tenant entitled to remove it?
options: No — anything left in place for the whole tenancy automatically becomes a fixture
Yes — with no real annexation and no purpose of permanently improving the property, it remains a chattel
No — only items the tenant personally paid for can ever be removed
Yes, but only if the landlord agrees in writing at the start of the lease
interaction.explanation: With no meaningful degree of annexation (it simply stands there) and no purpose of permanently improving the building, the bookcase remains a chattel under the Berkley v Poulett test and the tenant may remove it.

parts.heading: Bringing it together: grant, term and exit
parts.voice: synthesis — connects the lesson's three threads
body: The three ideas in this lesson connect directly. A lease exists as a legal estate under s 1(1)(b) LPA 1925 precisely because it is a term of years — a defined slice of time carved out of the freehold (or a superior lease) and given to a tenant with exclusive possession. That act of carving out the term for the first time is the grant; everything that happens to the lease afterwards, short of it ending, is dealt with by assignment rather than by a fresh grant.

The fixtures question sits at the far end of that same term: when the term of years finally ends — whether by expiry, surrender or forfeiture — the question of what the tenant may take away is really a question about where the legal estate's boundary sits. A fixture has become, in substance, part of the land itself and therefore part of what belongs to whoever holds the reversion; a chattel never crossed that line and always belonged to the tenant alone.

Holding the grant/assignment distinction and the fixtures test together gives you the full shape of a lease's life: how the legal estate is created, how it changes hands without being recreated, and what happens to what's inside it once the term is over — the three things every leasehold conveyancing transaction in this module ultimately turns on.

components.title: A lease's life: grant, dealings, and exit
components.description: How the term of years, grant/assignment distinction and fixtures rule fit together across a lease's life.

nodes.label: Grant: landlord creates a new term of years under s 1(1)(b) LPA 1925
Assignment: existing tenant transfers the running term to a new tenant, subject to any alienation clause
Term ends: outgoing tenant may remove chattels but must leave fixtures (Berkley v Poulett)

components.textAlternative: A lease begins with grant, where the landlord creates a brand-new term of years as a legal estate under s 1(1)(b) LPA 1925. During the term, the lease may be assigned from an existing tenant to a new one, subject to any alienation clause requiring landlord's consent, without a new estate being created. When the term ends, whether by expiry, surrender or forfeiture, the outgoing tenant may remove chattels but must leave fixtures behind, applying the Berkley v Poulett test.

interaction.prompt: Why does s 1(1)(b) LPA 1925 matter to the grant/assignment distinction covered earlier in this lesson?
options: It has no connection — grant and assignment are purely contractual concepts
It confirms that what is being granted or assigned (a term of years) is capable of existing as a legal estate in the first place, not merely a personal arrangement
It applies only to residential, not commercial, leases
It means every assignment automatically creates a new legal estate
interaction.explanation: Section 1(1)(b) is what makes a term of years a legal estate at all — capable of being granted, held, and then assigned as an estate in land, rather than existing only as a personal contractual licence between the original parties.

testPool.prompt: Which two estates does s 1(1) LPA 1925 recognise as capable of existing as legal estates in land?
options: Fee simple absolute in possession and term of years absolute
Fee simple absolute in possession and life interest
Term of years absolute and easement
Fee tail and term of years absolute
testPool.explanation: Section 1(1) lists only the fee simple absolute in possession (freehold) and the term of years absolute (leasehold) as capable of being legal estates; all other interests in land can exist only in equity.

testPool.prompt: What is the transaction called when a landlord creates a brand-new lease and gives it to a tenant for the first time?
options: Assignment
Grant
Surrender
Sub-letting
testPool.explanation: The grant of a lease is the creation of a new legal estate carved out of the landlord's freehold or superior interest — the transaction that brings the lease into existence.

testPool.prompt: What is the transaction called when an existing tenant transfers a running lease to a new tenant?
options: Grant
Assignment
Novation of the freehold
Registration
testPool.explanation: An assignment transfers an existing lease, with its remaining term, from the current tenant (assignor) to a new tenant (assignee) — no new legal estate is created.

testPool.prompt: A trainee describes a landlord's grant of a brand-new 25-year lease to a first-time tenant as 'assigning the lease to the tenant'. What is wrong with this description?
options: Nothing — grant and assignment are interchangeable terms
The word 'assign' is wrong because no lease existed before this transaction; the correct term is 'grant'
The description is wrong because the term should be described as a 'surrender'
It is only wrong if the lease is residential rather than commercial
testPool.explanation: Assignment presupposes an existing lease being transferred onward. Here no lease existed until the landlord created one, so the correct description is that the landlord has granted a new lease, not assigned an existing one.

testPool.prompt: A tenant with 12 years left on an existing 20-year lease wants to transfer the premises to a new occupier who will take over the lease as it stands, with the same rent and covenants. Which transaction is this?
options: A grant, because a new occupier is taking possession for the first time
An assignment, because an existing lease is being transferred rather than a new one created
A surrender, because the original tenant is giving up occupation
A sub-lease, because only part of the term remains
testPool.trapExplanation: It's tempting to focus on the fact that the new occupier has never held the premises before and call this a grant. What matters is not whether the new party is new to the property, but whether a new legal estate is being created — here it is not; the existing 20-year term simply changes hands.
testPool.explanation: Because the existing lease (with 12 years remaining) is being transferred rather than a new term created, this is an assignment, not a grant, regardless of whether the incoming party has occupied before.

testPool.prompt: A lease contains a covenant that the tenant must not assign without landlord's consent. The current tenant wants to transfer the lease to a new tenant. What must generally happen before the transfer can safely proceed?
options: Nothing — alienation clauses are unenforceable in modern leases
The current tenant must obtain the landlord's consent, typically formalised through a licence to assign
The lease must be terminated and a fresh lease granted to the new tenant instead
The new tenant must independently negotiate new lease terms with the landlord
testPool.trapExplanation: Some students assume an alienation clause means the lease simply cannot be assigned at all, or that it can be worked around by treating the transaction as a fresh grant. Neither is right — the clause conditions the assignment on consent, it does not prohibit it outright, and the underlying lease terms are not renegotiated.
testPool.explanation: An alienation clause requiring consent to assign is satisfied by the landlord's consent, usually formalised in a licence to assign — the existing lease is still assigned on its existing terms, not replaced with a new grant.

testPool.prompt: A trainee is told that, because a lease is 'only' a leasehold interest rather than a freehold, it cannot be a true legal estate in land. Is this correct?
options: Yes — only freehold can ever be a legal estate
No — a term of years absolute is expressly listed as a legal estate under s 1(1)(b) LPA 1925
It depends on whether the lease is registered at HM Land Registry
No, but only for leases granted for more than 99 years
testPool.trapExplanation: It's easy to assume 'legal estate' means freehold ownership and that leasehold is a lesser, merely contractual right. Section 1(1)(b) says otherwise: a term of years absolute stands alongside the fee simple absolute in possession as one of only two legal estates.
testPool.explanation: Section 1(1)(b) LPA 1925 expressly lists the term of years absolute as one of the two estates capable of existing as a legal estate — leasehold is not a lesser or merely equitable interest by virtue of being leasehold.

testPool.prompt: An outgoing tenant removes a built-in kitchen unit that was screwed to the wall and specifically designed and installed to fit that kitchen permanently. The landlord objects. Applying Berkley v Poulett, who is likely to be right?
options: The tenant — anything the tenant paid for personally can always be removed
The landlord — the degree of annexation and the purpose of permanently improving the property both point to this being a fixture
The tenant — items in a kitchen are always treated as chattels
The landlord, but only because the unit was screwed rather than merely resting in place
testPool.trapExplanation: Students often assume that who paid for an item settles ownership on departure. Berkley v Poulett does not ask who paid — it asks about the degree and purpose of annexation, both of which point towards a fitted, purpose-built kitchen unit being a fixture regardless of who funded it.
testPool.explanation: A unit screwed into place and designed specifically to improve the kitchen permanently satisfies both limbs of the Berkley v Poulett test — degree of annexation and purpose of annexation — making it a fixture the landlord is entitled to keep.

testPool.prompt: A tenant leaving a flat wants to remove curtains hung on a simple removable rail, and a fitted wardrobe built into an alcove and plastered around at the edges. Applying Berkley v Poulett, which is the tenant clearly entitled to take?
options: The curtains only
The fitted wardrobe only
Both
Neither
testPool.explanation: The curtains, hung on a simple removable rail with no real annexation and a purpose of being enjoyed as an item in their own right, remain a chattel. The fitted wardrobe, built into and plastered around the alcove, shows both real annexation and a purpose of permanently improving the space — making it a fixture that must stay.

testPool.prompt: Why did the court in Berkley v Poulett hold that the purpose of annexation had become the more important limb of the fixtures test, over degree of annexation alone?
options: Because degree of annexation is irrelevant and never considered
Because a heavy item can rest in place by its own weight, with no fixing at all, yet still be intended to improve the land permanently
Because purpose is easier for a court to measure objectively than degree
Because degree of annexation only matters for agricultural land
testPool.explanation: The case recognised that an item can be barely or not at all physically fixed and still be a fixture if placed there with the purpose of permanently improving the property — which is why purpose, not degree of physical attachment alone, does most of the real work in borderline cases.

testPool.prompt: What is the term used for the landlord's formal consent permitting a specific assignment of a lease to a specific new tenant?
options: A rent review memorandum
A licence to assign
A reversionary lease
A deed of variation
testPool.explanation: A licence to assign is the landlord's formal consent to a particular assignment, usually required by an alienation clause before the tenant may transfer the lease to the proposed new tenant.

testPool.prompt: Under s 1(1)(b) LPA 1925, what is the name given to the legal estate created when a lease is granted?
options: An equitable licence
A term of years absolute
A fee simple absolute in possession
A profit à prendre
testPool.explanation: Section 1(1)(b) names the leasehold legal estate a 'term of years absolute' — a defined maximum duration granted with exclusive possession.

testPool.prompt: A solicitor is instructed on a transaction and needs to decide whether it is governed by grant-stage drafting work or assignment-stage due diligence. What is the single most decisive question to ask first?
options: Whether the property is residential or commercial
Whether a lease already exists and is simply changing hands, or is being created for the first time
How many years remain on any existing lease
Whether the tenant is an individual or a company
testPool.explanation: The threshold question is whether a legal estate already exists and is merely being transferred (assignment) or is being brought into existence for the first time (grant) — everything else about the appropriate conveyancing approach follows from that answer.

testPool.prompt: A landlord and a prospective tenant are negotiating rent, repairing obligations and a break clause for premises the tenant has never previously occupied, with no lease yet in existence. Which stage of leasehold conveyancing does this describe, and what statutory basis makes the resulting document a legal estate?
options: Assignment; s 27 LRA 2002
Grant; s 1(1)(b) LPA 1925
Surrender; s 52 LPA 1925
Sub-letting; s 1(1)(a) LPA 1925
testPool.explanation: Negotiating terms for a lease that does not yet exist is the grant stage, and once granted, the resulting term of years is capable of existing as a legal estate because of s 1(1)(b) LPA 1925.

debriefConfig.trapSummary: The recurring error in this lesson's items is treating grant and assignment as interchangeable labels for 'someone gets a lease', and treating the fixtures test as turning on who paid for an item rather than on its degree and purpose of annexation. Both distinctions are the ones the rest of the leasehold module assumes you already have solid.
